analysis.one_liner: Restricts Medicare drug middlemen (PBMs) to flat service fees and requires transparent reporting on pharmacy payments.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with support from senators in both parties, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2025 and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are companies that insurance plans hire to run drug benefits: they negotiate with drugmakers, decide which pharmacies are in the network, and decide what pharmacies get paid. This bill would bar PBMs in Medicare's drug program from making money on anything other than flat, disclosed service fees — ending practices like pocketing the difference between what the plan pays and what they pay the pharmacy, or taking fees tied to drug prices. It would also require plans to let any qualifying pharmacy into their networks, let pharmacies file complaints about unfair contract terms with federal penalties behind them, force PBMs to report detailed data on drug costs and their own profits each year, and require Medicare to track 'essential' pharmacies — the only pharmacy for miles — to see if they are being squeezed out of business.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who pay drug copays, and the independent and community pharmacies that serve them — including rural and small-town pharmacies that are the last one around. PBMs have faced lawsuits and federal scrutiny over practices like spread pricing (keeping part of what the insurer pays for a drug instead of passing it to the pharmacy) and steering patients to PBM-owned pharmacies; this bill targets exactly those practices. Pharmacies also gain the right to file complaints about unfair contract terms and protection from retaliation for doing so.

how_it_helps.text: Bars PBMs from taking any income other than flat, fair-market service fees, and requires them to disgorge other remuneration to plans — closing the spread between what insurers pay PBMs and what PBMs pay pharmacies.

Requires plans to accept any willing pharmacy that meets standard contract terms, and lets pharmacies file federal complaints when plan contract terms are not reasonable, with anti-retaliation protections and civil penalties.

Requires PBMs to report detailed annual data — dispensing volumes, reimbursement, affiliate pharmacy pricing, and generic versus brand coverage decisions — to plans and to CMS, and gives plans the right to audit their PBM annually.

Requires CMS to publish a public list of 'essential retail pharmacies' — pharmacies that are the only one within 1 to 10 miles depending on area — and report every two years on how they are paid and whether they are staying open.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliates — including PBM-owned pharmacies — who would lose income from spread pricing, price-based fees, and rebate-related revenue, and would face new audit, reporting, and penalty exposure. Insurers (PDP sponsors) face some compliance costs and potential penalties, though PBMs must reimburse them for penalties tied to delegated work.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is largely complaint-driven: pharmacies must file allegations through a new federal process, limited to once per plan year per contract unless the contract is modified, so a pharmacy afraid of losing its main payer may be hesitant to use it.

The key standards — what counts as a fair 'bona fide service fee' and whether contract terms are 'reasonable and relevant' — are left to future regulations by the Secretary, so the bill's real-world effect depends on rules not yet written and could be weaker than advertised.
The bill adds a large new reporting and audit burden on PBMs and plans, which insurers argue could raise administrative costs that ultimately feed into Medicare premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits are real but partly deferred to rulemaking: the flat-fee rule strikes directly at the largest source of PBMs' spread revenue, and "any willing pharmacy" plus federal enforcement give independent pharmacies a genuine remedy against unfair contract terms, which matters in areas where losing the last pharmacy means long drives for medicine. The costs fall on PBMs and insurers, though some compliance cost could ultimately flow into Medicare premiums. The main weakness is design risk: enforcement depends on individual pharmacies filing allegations and on the Secretary writing strong contract standards, and the bill's heavy reporting regime could favor the largest PBMs if small ones cannot absorb compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it sits there with no vote.

narrative.text: The Senate introduced the bill on March 6, 2025 and read it twice.
The same day it was referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which is where the bill's action history ends.
As of the latest record, no markup, floor vote, or further action has been scheduled or taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PBM middlemen, who keep their current fee and rebate structures, are better off because the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBM middlemen keep the status quo

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled an initial bipartisan group of cosponsors.

for.name: Senate Committee on Finance
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 6, 2025 and has taken no action on it since.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has 7 cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans alongside its Republican sponsor, so it is one of the few PBM bills with backing from both parties — but it is still waiting for a committee to move it.

industries.note: The bill would end the main non-flat-fee ways PBMs earn money in Medicare Part D — spread pricing, retained rebates, and volume-based fees — and expose their affiliated pharmacies' pricing to federal reporting and audit. This is the industry the bill is explicitly aimed at.

Any-willing-pharmacy participation, federal contract standards, a complaint process with anti-retaliation protection, and public tracking of the last pharmacy in underserved areas all directly address the contract terms and closures that have driven independent pharmacies out of business.

Insurers face new penalties and reporting duties, but they also gain the right to claw back PBM remuneration and audit their PBMs. The bill leaves plans themselves largely in charge of pharmacy contracting.

Rebates remain legal if fully passed through to plans, but the bill requires written explanations of rebate deals contingent on formulary placement and reporting on plans that favor brand drugs over cheaper generics or biosimilars — pressure on a system that has benefited brand manufacturers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since March 2025 with no markup or floor action scheduled. PBM bills have attracted broad bipartisan interest this Congress, so the committee could fold these provisions into a larger Medicare or PBM package; on its own, the bill is likely to die quietly at the end of the Congress unless leadership prioritizes it.
